title: Testing a Claim about a Proportion
short: Carry out a one-proportion z test.
trouble: Students write hypotheses about the sample statistic instead of the population parameter.

blocks.html: Now carry out a complete test for a proportion, using the logic of significance tests. The steps are always the same: hypotheses, conditions, test statistic, p-value, conclusion in context.

To test $H_0: p = p_0$: $$z = \dfrac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{\dfrac{p_0(1 - p_0)}{n}}}.$$ The p-value is the area beyond z in the direction of $H_a$ (both tails if $H_a$ is $\ne$). Conditions: a random sample, and $np_0 \ge 10$ and $n(1 - p_0) \ge 10$.

The test asks how surprising $\hat{p}$ would be if $H_0$ were true. In that world the true proportion is $p_0$, so the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ is centered at $p_0$ with SD $\sqrt{p_0(1 - p_0)/n}$, computed with $p_0$, not $\hat{p}$. (A confidence interval has no claimed value to use, which is why it uses $\hat{p}$.) The z-score measures how many of those SDs $\hat{p}$ sits from $p_0$.

blocks.name: normal
blocks.cap: The one-sided p-value for z = 1.85 is the area to the right.

blocks.title: A complete test
blocks.q: Last year 30% of students walked to school. This year, in a random sample of 200 students, 72 walk. Is there convincing evidence that the proportion has gone up? Use $\alpha = 0.05$. ($P(Z < 1.85) = 0.9678$.)
steps: Hypotheses: $H_0: p = 0.3$, $H_a: p > 0.3$, where $p$ is this year's proportion of all students who walk.
Conditions: random sample; $200(0.3) = 60$ and $200(0.7) = 140$ are at least 10.
$0.0322 < 0.05$: reject $H_0$. There is convincing evidence that more than 30% of students walk this year.

blocks.title: A one-sided test the other way
blocks.q: A seed company claims 85% of its seeds sprout. A gardener plants 400 and 328 sprout. Test the claim against $H_a: p < 0.85$ at $\alpha = 0.05$. ($P(Z < -1.68) = 0.0465$.)
steps: Reject $H_0$: there is convincing (though not overwhelming) evidence that fewer than 85% sprout.

blocks.html: Writing the hypotheses about the sample statistic: "$H_0: \hat{p} = 0.3$." We already know $\hat{p} = 0.36$; there is nothing to test about it. Hypotheses are always about the population parameter $p$. Check that your hypotheses use $p$ and the claimed value, never the sample result.
